title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A Session with MBA Students at Georgetown University – March 4, 2021
summary: Pabrai recounts the accidental 1999 start of Pabrai Funds and the major 2020 shift in his approach after reading Nick Sleep's Nomad letters, from buying discounted pies to owning growing pies with a founder's mindset. He covers hunting for cheap markets in Korea, Turkey and Japan, checklist lessons from leverage failures like Delta Financial, the 0/6/25 fee structure and 'McDonald's sign' investor selection, the theater-on-fire model behind Seritage, Dakshana, and why he now does nothing as long as a business keeps getting better.

ideas.idea: Pabrai Funds started accidentally as a hobby in July 1999 with $1 million from eight friends, cloning the Buffett partnership rules of the 1950s.
ideas.detail: No management fee, a 6% hurdle and annual redemptions; the fund was up over 70% the first year, reached about $2.5 million by late 2000, and he then decided to treat it as a real business.

ideas.idea: Investing knowledge is cumulative, so you must be a continuous learning machine and can keep improving into your seventies and eighties.
ideas.detail: Unlike athletes, investors get better as they pile on years, learning especially from mistakes and from other investors, and the model changes periodically.

ideas.idea: Reading Nick Sleep's Nomad letters in 2020 caused a significant change: think about ownership stakes the way a founding family would, which stretches time horizons and is more tax efficient.
ideas.detail: Instead of buying discounted pies at 50-60% off intrinsic value, he now focuses on growing pies, long-term compounders that can scale, even if they require paying a bit more. He recommends Googling 'Nick Sleep Nomad letters'.

ideas.idea: With US stocks priced to perfection in 2019-2021, he broadened to entire markets that were cheap and unloved like Japan, Korea and Turkey, visiting portfolios of trusted local Graham-Munger investors.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Week-long trips to Seoul cover 15-20 businesses from a friend's portfolio; cloning such ideas is powerful because they have already passed one set of filters. He now has investments in Turkey and Korea, and a China trip was cancelled by COVID.

ideas.idea: In very cheap markets the temptation is to buy anything at 3x earnings rather than the better businesses at 8-9x, and he is trying to move his Turkish friend from Graham to Munger.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Cultural nuances about how owners and managers think are an overlay, but a business is a business anywhere: discount future cash flows.

ideas.idea: The best lessons come from losers, so his pre-investment checklist, built about 13 years ago from great investors' mistakes, clusters around leverage, misunderstood moats, and management/ownership issues.
ideas.detail: Leverage was the largest category of mistakes where visible pre-investment data should have given pause. He has had multiple 100% losses from leverage and is much leerier of heavily indebted companies.

ideas.idea: Delta Financial, a sensible mortgage underwriter, went to zero in late 2007 when securitizations stopped and it was caught with mortgages on its warehouse lines, costing about $50-60 million.
ideas.detail: The originate-securitize-repeat model needed little equity and was very profitable until the music stopped; he has not touched a mortgage company since and does not plan to.

ideas.idea: Moats show up in the numbers over long periods, and the challenge is that great businesses are usually fully priced, so wait for misunderstanding or temporary headwinds to decimate the price.
ideas.detail: Picking up MasterCard's numbers is enough to see it is a great business; sifting great from not-great is not hard.

ideas.idea: Large inheritances are a disservice to your gene pool, so surplus wealth should be recycled to society seeking a high social return on invested capital.
ideas.detail: Buffett's line: Jesse Owens's son does not become a great sprinter by starting at the 40-meter line, though the 5-meter line is fine. Dakshana, started in 2006 with his wife, gives free prep to very poor bright Indian kids, and several thousand have entered the IITs and top medical schools.

ideas.idea: P/E is an inadequate metric; a portfolio at 23x forward earnings is not expensive if the businesses grow 20-30% a year for 5-10 years, and market trends and macro should be ignored.
ideas.detail: Per Nick Sleep, you could have paid 100x earnings for Walmart in the 1970s or even 1980s and still beaten the market; Walmart's public runway has lasted 51 years and only the Walton family held it throughout.

ideas.idea: Start a fund with the 0/6/25 structure from day one, and first prove yourself by building your own wealth, because Munger's first criterion for a manager is financial independence.
ideas.detail: Li Lu turned the float on his student loans into over $1 million by graduation. Pabrai sold part of his business for about $1 million in 1994 and had over $10 million by 1999, and investors came to him. Many of his investors refuse managers who charge 1-2% fees.

ideas.idea: Your fund's rules act like a McDonald's sign: no investor calls, no quarterly calls, just a website, which filtered his base to principals and first-generation entrepreneurs rather than agents.
ideas.detail: University endowments moved on quickly when given only a website login. Investors in New Zealand wired several million dollars without ever meeting or calling him; the fund has 350-400 families and one annual meeting.

ideas.idea: You need no opinion on 99% of securities; look only at what is inside your circle of competence, products you use and things around you.
ideas.detail: If you understand a business you know what it is worth and can see the delta to price. Before buying, you should be able to explain to a nine-year-old in five sentences why you will be drowning in wealth and cannot lose money.

ideas.idea: The stock market is a theater where every seat must always be occupied, so when someone yells fire the ticket clears at whatever price gets a new buyer to sit down.
ideas.detail: Seritage traded at $35-40 before COVID and instantly went to $6-9; Pabrai bought a bit more than one-eighth of all the seats and says the movie is great even if it is a little warm under his seat. He will discuss it fully once he no longer owns it.

ideas.idea: Don't trim or sell a great business because it hits or exceeds intrinsic value; the only question is whether the business is getting better.
ideas.detail: Worth 100 and trading at 120 is an irrelevant data point; 20x fair and 30x actual is not a reason to sell into a 12x alternative given taxes. Only something egregious like Snowflake at 80x sales is a different conversation. He used to sell at intrinsic value and buy something else, and no longer does.

ideas.idea: Be comfortable with 95% of the portfolio in one stock if it is a great business that keeps getting better, like Amazon held for 15 years.
ideas.detail: Amazon is getting better by the day and is not egregiously overvalued; Jeff Bezos says it is still day one, so he would wait until day two to reconsider.

ideas.idea: Four or five stocks is enough for your own money, per Munger; with other people's money he caps positions around 10%, and 10 stocks is plenty.
ideas.detail: Nobody should own 20 or 30 stocks. Pabrai Funds rarely puts more than 10% into anything because it is other people's money.

ideas.idea: You only truly understand a business after you own it with real money, so starting small and adding as the price rises, as Li Lu and Nick Sleep do, is a valid approach.
ideas.detail: Li Lu believes risk goes down the longer you own a business because knowledge grows. Nick Sleep ran about 30 stocks with seven or eight making up 70-80% and a 'farm team' of small positions that might be promoted.

ideas.idea: Low disclosure in emerging markets does not preclude conviction if you understand the product, moat and economics and the track record shows it; otherwise have the discipline to pass.
ideas.detail: Disclosure and understanding are not directly correlated; he does not invest without great conviction, and the range of alternatives is large enough to walk away.

ideas.idea: What happens in the market is irrelevant; even when his portfolio fell two-thirds in the financial crisis his demeanor did not change, because panics are when tickets get discounted.
ideas.detail: 'If wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost.' Businesses go on sale either from company-specific hiccups or when a hundred theaters are on fire at once.
